title: The delta Scuti pulsations of HD 303514 come from its third star: TESS pulsation phases show no 19.9-day orbit, and their Doppler shifts follow the 598-day eclipse-timing orbit
abstract: HD 303514 is a 19.9-day eclipsing binary whose eclipses faded from 2002 to 2026. Other campaign studies found a third body on a 1.6-year orbit from eclipse times and depths, but no study detected the third star directly. In our own TESS full-frame photometry (8 sectors, 2019-2026) we found delta Scuti pulsations at 8.534, 9.334 and 10.053 cycles per day. Per-pixel pulsation and eclipse maps agree (correlation 0.994; centroids within 1.2-2.1 arcsec; the only bright neighbour is 13.8 arcsec away), so the pulsator is in HD 303514. The pulsation phases show no light-travel delay across the 19.9-day orbit (-20 +- 12 s and +12 +- 10 s, against +-57 s expected; an injection test recovers 54.5 s), so the pulsator is not in the eclipsing pair. Between sectors all modes shift by the same fraction: one Doppler shift per sector fits (chi-square 5.8 for 14 degrees of freedom), constant frequencies do not (42.9 for 21). The velocities range from -35 to +36 km/s. A three-body model fitted only to TESS eclipse times and geometry predicts these velocities with chi-square 7.5 against 28.9 for a constant, with a fitted scale of 0.92 +- 0.20 (1 is expected for the third star; about -0.55 for a pair star). Thus the third star is the delta Scuti pulsator and its velocity curve is measured from photometry. A joint REBOUND model of 18 TESS times, impact parameters, ASAS-3 photometry (2001-2009) and the velocities gives P2 = 598.1 (596.5-599.7) d, e2 = 0.23, m3/M12 = 0.66 (0.59-0.75), mutual inclination 4.0 deg and K3 = 29.3 km/s for a fixed pair mass of 4 solar masses. This repeats the parallel campaign results. In 57 of 60 posterior draws the eclipses do not stop before 2060; the TESS depth reaches a minimum of 0.08 (0.03-0.16) percent near 2035. Limits: twin point-mass pair with fixed mass and radius scale, velocity errors of 9-25 km/s, possible intrinsic frequency changes, a short MCMC, no spectra, and a tension between the dynamical third-star mass and its light.

citations.reason: Source study: found the fading eclipses of HD 303514. We use its TESS linear ephemeris, secondary phase and radius scale. Our model does not support its eclipse loss near 2030.
Curved precession forecast of eclipse loss near 2030-2032; our posterior gives loss before 2060 in 5 percent of draws.
Prior campaign work on orbital-plane changes in TESS eclipsing binaries (HD 93683) that started this line of work.
Parallel study: 593-day third body from TESS eclipse times. Our pulsation velocities confirm the orbit independently; our forecast does not support its eclipse loss near 2030.
Parallel study: 584-600-day near-coplanar third body from own TESS cutout times and no eclipse loss before 2060; we repeat these results and add a direct velocity detection of the third star.
Parallel study: ASAS-3 eclipse times confirm the third body; m3 = 1.8-4.1 solar masses for a 4-solar-mass pair, consistent with our m3/M12.
Parallel study: ASAS-3 eclipse times support the 592-day third body and shallowest eclipses in 2030-2035 without loss.
Parallel study: 595-day cycle and apsidal motion in ASAS-3; m3/M12 = 0.52, below our 0.66.
Parallel study: Harvard plates of 1889-1955 agree with the three-body model and reject eclipse-loss histories.
Planned spectroscopic velocity tests of HD 303514 states; our pulsation velocities give a photometric version of this test.
